\chapter{Medicine and Keeping Well}
\label{ch:ml-medicine}
\hlchaptermodality{107}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name medicine, treatment and cleanliness, and place them around the symptoms I can already say.}

From cold: three words around falling ill, and which one Malayalam did not have to borrow.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[marunnŭ]{\ml{മരുന്ന്} — medicine}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-marunnu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{fever}. Say \emph{a doctor}. You have had both for a long while, and nothing at all to put between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} (\emph{marunnŭ}) — \textbf{medicine}.

You can already name what is wrong — the cough, the pain, the tiredness, the fever — and you can name the person you would go to. \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} is the thing that was missing in the middle.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{This one is not borrowed.} It is an old Dravidian word, and Tamil says \emph{marundhu} for the same thing. The remedy has a native name.

That is worth holding on to, because the \textbf{next} word in this chapter — the one for the treatment itself — came from Sanskrit. The substance is named in Malayalam's own words; the practice is named in borrowed ones.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item the fever, then the medicine, then the doctor
  \item which language this word comes from, and what Tamil says
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Medicine? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) Who would you go to for it? (\textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}}.) Is this word borrowed? (\textbf{No} — it is Dravidian, and Tamil has it too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cikitsa]{\ml{ചികിത്സ} — treatment}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-chikitsa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{medicine}. Say \emph{a doctor}. One of those is a thing; the other is a person. Neither is what happens between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} (\emph{cikitsa}) — \textbf{treatment}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} & \emph{vaidyan} & the person \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} & \emph{cikitsa} & what the person does \\
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{marunnŭ} & what the person gives \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Keep the caveat \texttt{ML-C48-doctor} gave you.} That lesson said \textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} in Kerala today usually points at a practitioner of the traditional medicine, and that the everyday word for a hospital doctor is the English one worn down into Malayalam sounds. So this row of three is one of the two pictures Kerala keeps side by side, not both of them — and it is the one that has Malayalam words for all three parts.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Sanskrit, where the last word was Dravidian — and do not read a rule into that.} This book has told you the opposite tendency twice: that Malayalam took \textbf{far more Sanskrit into everyday speech} than Tamil did, and that when a native verb narrowed, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}a Sanskrit word took each vacated slot\textquotedblright{}}. Borrowing here is the norm, not the formal exception.

What this small set shows is narrower and more interesting: of the three words this chapter gives you, \textbf{two are borrowed and one is not}, and the one that is not is the substance you swallow.

The Sanskrit is \textbf{\dv{चिकित्सा}} \emph{cikitsā} — Malayalam drops the long final vowel. It is built from the root \textbf{√cit}, \emph{to perceive}, in the \textbf{desiderative}: a regular Sanskrit formation meaning \emph{wanting to}. So the word is assembled as something like \textbf{a wish to see clearly}, and that derivation is the standard one in the reference grammars rather than a folk story.
\end{culture}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{One join in this word is new, and it is new as a pair, not as a shape.} Every letter in \textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} is one you have written. What you have not seen before is \textbf{\ml{ത}} and \textbf{\ml{സ}} joined:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ത}} & \emph{ta} & \texttt{ML-S08-letter-ta} \\
\textbf{\ml{്}} & chandrakkala & \texttt{ML-W01-sa-chandrakkala-ka} \\
\textbf{\ml{സ}} & \emph{sa} & \texttt{ML-S124-letter-sa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is the same machine \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} showed you on your first day: put the chandrakkala on the first consonant to strip its inherent \emph{a}, then set the next consonant behind it. There \textbf{\ml{സ്}} met \textbf{\ml{ക}}; here \textbf{\ml{ത്}} meets \textbf{\ml{സ}}. Read \textbf{\ml{ചി}-\ml{കി}-\ml{ത്}-\ml{സ}} slowly, then at speed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cikitsa}
  \item the three together — \emph{vaidyan}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item which of the three is the native word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Treatment? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}}.) Of \textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} and \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}, which is borrowed? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}}.) Which one is the substance? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vṛtti]{\ml{വൃത്തി} — cleanliness}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-vrtthi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{medicine}, then \emph{treatment}. Both of those come after something has gone wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} (\emph{vṛtti}) — \textbf{cleanliness}.

\textbf{This is the everyday word, and it is worth being plain about its range.} It is what you use about a room, a kitchen, a person's hands. Malayalam's formal word for hygiene as a subject — the kind printed on a public notice — is \emph{śucitvaṁ}, given here in sound only, because this book has not taught it. \textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} is the one people say.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The Sanskrit it comes from does not mean clean at all.} \emph{vṛtti} is built on the root \textbf{√vṛt}, \emph{to turn, to proceed} — so \emph{a way of going on}: conduct, and also \textbf{livelihood}.

\textbf{Malayalam did not narrow it; it added a sense and kept the rest.} The word is still current for an occupation, and the older sense shows through in the everyday \textbf{\ml{വൃത്തികെട്ട}} — \emph{filthy} — which is literally \emph{of spoiled conduct}.

How \emph{a way of going on} came to mean \emph{how clean you keep things} is a short step if you have ever been told that a clean house is a matter of character. Take that road as the traditional account rather than a settled fact; both senses are well attested, and it is the path between them that is told rather than proved.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vṛtti}
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}, then \emph{vṛtti} — the medicine, and the thing that comes before needing one
  \item what the Sanskrit word behind it meant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cleanliness? (\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}}.) What does the Sanskrit root behind it mean? (\textbf{To turn, to proceed} — so \emph{a way of going on}.) Of this chapter's three words, which is the native one? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\ml{വൃത്തി}, \ml{ചികിത്സ} — on either side of falling ill}

\label{lesson:ML-C107-before-and-after}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{fever}. Say \emph{cough}. Those are the middle of the story.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Lay this chapter out against what you already had and it makes a line:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} & \emph{vṛtti} & \textbf{before} — keeping well \\
\textbf{\ml{പനി}}, \textbf{\ml{ചുമ}} & \emph{pani}, \emph{cuma} & the thing going wrong \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}}, \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ} & \textbf{after} — getting well \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two of those five are native and three are borrowed}, and it is not the split you would guess: \textbf{\ml{പനി}} and \textbf{\ml{ചുമ}}, the two you have had longest, are the Dravidian ones — their own lessons say so — and \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} joins them from this chapter.

\textbf{You have had the middle of that line for a long while, and the far end only as a person.} You could say what was wrong, and name \textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} — but not one word for what they would actually do, or give, or for the keeping-well that comes before any of it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the line in order — \emph{vṛtti}, \emph{pani}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{marunnŭ}
  \item which of the four words in that line you have had the longest
  \item the person who stands at the far end — \emph{vaidyan}
  \item which of \emph{vṛtti}, \emph{cikitsa} and \emph{marunnŭ} is not borrowed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word comes \textbf{before} falling ill? (\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}}.) Which two come \textbf{after}? (\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} and \textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) Which of those two is the substance? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[marunnŭ enna ōrmma]{(medicine, treatment, cleanliness) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R107-medicine-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{medicine}, \emph{treatment} and \emph{cleanliness}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one native word among three}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}} & \emph{marunnŭ} & \textbf{Dravidian} — Tamil says \emph{marundhu} \\
\textbf{\ml{ചികിത്സ}} & \emph{cikitsa} & Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} & \emph{vṛtti} & Sanskrit, and it meant \textbf{conduct} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The thing you swallow kept its own name; the practice and the virtue came in from Sanskrit.} Do not read a rule into it — this book has told you that Malayalam took \textbf{far more Sanskrit into everyday speech} than Tamil did. What is true of these three is true of these three: two borrowed, one not, and the one that is not is the substance.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You had the symptoms and the person, and nothing in between.} \textbf{\ml{പനി}} and \textbf{\ml{വേദന}} came with the other words for feeling unwell, and \textbf{\ml{വൈദ്യൻ}} came with the words for what people do — so you could say what was wrong and who you would see, and nothing about what would be done.

\textbf{You have had one end of it longer than you think}: \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}}, well-being, has been yours since you first asked somebody how they were. What this chapter adds is the keeping of it, and the mending when it goes.

Now the line runs end to end: keep clean, fall ill, be treated, take the medicine.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{marunnŭ}, \emph{cikitsa}, \emph{vṛtti}
  \item which one is Dravidian
  \item what \emph{vṛtti} meant in Sanskrit
  \item the whole line, from keeping well to taking the medicine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Medicine, treatment, cleanliness? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}, \ml{ചികിത്സ}, \ml{വൃത്തി}}.) Which one did Malayalam not have to borrow? (\textbf{\ml{മരുന്ന്}}.) What did \textbf{\ml{വൃത്തി}} mean before it meant clean? (\textbf{Conduct}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
